match.reason: No existing point covers what drives exchange rate movements; related points like the balance of payments, net trade and monetary policy touch on currencies but do not teach the causes of Australian dollar changes.

draft.title: What moves the Australian dollar
card: The Australian dollar floats, so its price changes when demand for it or supply of it changes. Anything that makes foreigners want more Australian dollars pushes the price up.
Commodity prices
Australia exports a lot of commodities such as iron ore and coal. When their prices rise, foreign buyers need more Australian dollars to pay for them, and the dollar tends to rise.
Interest rates
If Australian interest rates rise compared with other countries, investors can earn more here. They buy Australian dollars to invest, and the dollar tends to rise.
Confidence and speculation

Investors tend to buy the dollar when they are confident about Australia's economy. Speculators buy or sell it to profit from the changes they expect, and this can push the dollar further the same way.
draft.remember: Anything that raises foreign demand for Australian dollars tends to lift the dollar. Anything that lowers it tends to pull the dollar down.

a.q: The world price of iron ore rises sharply. What is the most likely effect on the Australian dollar?
opts: It rises, as buyers need more Australian dollars
It falls, as buyers need fewer Australian dollars
It rises, as Australia imports more iron ore
It falls, as Australian interest rates drop
a.why: Australia exports iron ore, so higher prices mean foreign buyers need more Australian dollars to pay for it. Demand for the dollar rises, so the dollar tends to rise. The idea that it falls reverses cause and effect.
a.clue: Who needs Australian dollars to buy iron ore?

b.q: Overseas interest rates rise while Australian rates stay the same. Investors expect higher returns abroad. What is the most likely effect on the Australian dollar?
opts: It tends to fall, as demand for it weakens
It tends to rise, as demand for it strengthens
It tends to rise, as Australian rates are now lower
It stays the same, as Australian rates did not change
b.why: Australian rates are now lower compared with other countries, so investors shift money abroad and buy fewer Australian dollars. Demand falls, so the dollar tends to fall. Australian rates not changing does not matter, because it is the gap between rates that moves the dollar.
b.clue: Look at the difference between rates, not just Australia's rate.

a.best: It rises, as buyers need more Australian dollars

b.best: It tends to fall, as demand for it weakens

problems.detail: The first bullet restates point 1's idea (the dollar floats and is priced by supply and demand) instead of only mentioning it.
Why (a) says the 'falls' answer 'reverses cause and effect'. That option actually gets the direction of the effect wrong, not the order of cause and effect, so the explanation could confuse students.

proposal.title: What moves the Australian dollar
card: Four main forces move the floating Australian dollar: commodity prices, interest rate differences, confidence and speculation. Each works by changing how many Australian dollars foreigners want to buy.
Commodity prices
Australia exports a lot of commodities such as iron ore and coal. When their prices rise, foreign buyers need more Australian dollars to pay for them, and the dollar tends to rise.
Interest rates
If Australian interest rates rise compared with other countries, investors can earn more here and buy Australian dollars, so the dollar tends to rise. If the gap shrinks, the dollar tends to fall.
Confidence and speculation

Investors tend to buy the dollar when they are confident about Australia's economy. Speculators buy or sell it to profit from the changes they expect, and this can push the dollar further the same way.
proposal.remember: Anything that raises foreign demand for Australian dollars tends to lift the dollar. Anything that lowers it tends to pull the dollar down.
